It is hard to believe it’s been almost 70 years since Dick Clark stepped onto the set of “American Bandstand” for the first time. The music and dance showcase ran for more than three decades. On the show, Clark, who was both host and producer, played the biggest hits of the day. For the premiere, in August 1957, there was none bigger than Buddy Holly’s “That’ll Be The Day.”

The song, written by Holly and Jerry Allison, was the best-selling of Holly’s foreshortened career. It reached No. 1 in both the U.S. and the U.K.

The inspiration for the song came from an unlikely source. Holly, his brother Larry, and his writing partner Allison went to see the great American Western “The Searchers,” starring John Wayne. In it, Wayne repeatedly uttered the phrase “that’ll be the day.” Holly couldn’t get the line out of his head. So he put it to music.

Though Holly died at the incredibly young age of 22, he is considered a pioneer of rock ‘n’ roll. The number of rockers and pop stars who have covered “That’ll Be The Day” is testament to that. One of the first was the Quarrymen. You may not have heard of the Liverpool band, but you likely know what they became: the Beatles.
